note: Separates intrinsic from extrinsic bias and organises evaluation by data, model and output level.
title: Bias in Large Language Models: Origin, Evaluation, and Mitigation
explain_beginner: This paper asks where bias in large language models actually comes from, not just whether it exists. Most people know that chatbots can produce stereotyped or unfair text, but this survey tries to trace that back to its source. It splits the causes into two kinds, bias built into the model itself from how it was trained, called intrinsic bias, and bias that only shows up once the model is used for a specific task, called extrinsic bias. Intrinsic bias comes from things like which groups are over or under represented in the training text, from data scraped mostly from English speaking, Western sources, and from ambiguous language where gender neutral words get silently associated with one gender. Extrinsic bias shows up later, for example in how a model resolves pronouns or judges sentiment differently depending on the names or groups mentioned in a task. The paper finds that these two sources need different tests and different fixes. It does not resolve the field's biggest open question, whether bias can be fully removed rather than just measured and reduced, and the authors say directly that the problem stays complex and ongoing as models keep changing.
explain_business: For a team choosing how to test or fix bias in a deployed model, this paper is useful mainly as an inventory rather than a specific recommendation. It shows that data level fixes, curating or rebalancing training data, and post model fixes, filtering or adjusting output after generation, are different levers, so a vendor who says they mitigated bias needs to specify at which stage, since a post processing filter does nothing to repair biased internal representations and vice versa. The practical risk this surfaces is the accuracy fairness tradeoff the authors flag, meaning a business that pushes hard on one fairness metric without checking task accuracy could ship a model that is measurably fairer on paper but worse at the actual job. There is no finished product or standard here, this is a map of research directions as of late 2024, not a compliance framework. It becomes operationally relevant once a company needs to justify to auditors, customers, or regulators which of these four evaluation levels and three mitigation stages its own testing actually covers, since most vendor bias claims today only test one of the four.
explain_practitioner: The paper organizes evaluation into four levels, data level checks looking at representation, imbalance, and source skew in the training corpus, model level checks using fairness metrics like equal opportunity and predictive parity plus interpretability tools such as SHAP and LIME, output level checks comparing outputs across counterfactual inputs and scoring stereotype and toxicity content, and a fourth human involved level using expert review. On mitigation it lays out three stages, pre model methods like counterfactual data augmentation and resampling, intra model methods like dropout regularization and causal inference during training, and post model methods applied after training such as Self Debias, SENT DEBIAS, INLP, and causal prompting. Rather than proposing one new method, it maps which techniques exist at each stage and what they target. The authors' own stated limitation matters here, they note that biases are context dependent and shift over time, that model scale makes comprehensive identification harder, and that fixing bias often trades off against accuracy, so a technique that reduces one measured bias can quietly hurt task performance elsewhere.
